newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Opposition blockades Serbian city in TV dispute.
newsitem.headline: Opposition blockades Serbian city in TV dispute.

text.p: Opposition protesters blocked roads into the central Serbian city of Kragujevac on Thursday after Socialist Party (SPS) authorities defeated in elections refused to hand over the regional radio and television centre.

Some 10,000 supporters of the incoming Zajedno (Together) coalition local government had surrounded the building on Wednesday and planned similar action later on Thursday after a road blockade scheduled to last three hours.

Traffic chaos enveloped the industrial city of 200,000 after Zajedno activists sealed off main and side roads into town. Motorists detoured onto mud tracks and across fields in desperate efforts to make their way.

Protests broke out in Kragujevac after security police "occupied" the radio and TV building on Wednesday morning to allow SPS management to keep broadcasting while the party tried to tie up a handover to Zajedno in the courts.

Analysts said the Kragujevac row was a textbook example of SPS resistance to democratic reform dramatised by its annulment of municipal elections in 14 cities won by the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition.

The SPS, led by President Slobodan Milosevic, knows that ceding power in municipalities, with their control of key media outlets and most courts, would spell the end to monolithic leftist rule in federal Yugoslavia dating to 1945.

Kragujevac was not one of the 14 cities where voting was nullified. Zajedno handily won Kragujevac without SPS allegations of "irregularities", the pretext for annulments elsewhere, and has already convened its municipal assembly.

But Socialists anxious to keep Serbia's major media organs in their hands were manoeuvring to avoid losing the Kragujevac station (RTK), an important news broadcaster in the central hinterland some 100 km (65 miles) south of Belgrade.

"The situation was pretty explosive overnight. People were on the verge of breaking into the building because they fear the Socialists' behaviour is foot-dragging that could last forever (unless we fight back)," said Nenad Vasiljevic, a Zajedno coalition committee member in Kragujevac.

Beta said that when the SPS realised it would lose last November's vote in Kragujevac, it hastily enacted legislation under which RTK would be merged with the national, SPS-run Radio and Television Serbia (RTS).
A Belgrade court quashed the measure on appeal, saying the right of the new Zajedno-dominated city assembly to appoint new management at the Kragujevac station took precedence.
Local sources said the SPS eventually agreed to formally vacate RTK at 8 a.m. on Wednesday but instead had dozens of loyal police occupy it to thwart a handover.
RTS, meanwhile, appealed to a higher court and sent two managers from Belgrade to run the Kragujevac station.
Independent local media said Zajedno did not intend to turn Kragujevac radio and TV into its own media organ but merely open its programming to a variety of news and opinion.
Zajedno is committed to democratic and free-market reform in Serbia, in part by liberalising the media and judiciary.
Daily demonstrations by students and Zajedno demanding that the government reinstate opposition victories in all 14 cities in dispute are now in their 10th week.
Milosevic has not deigned to acknowledge the opposition triumphs despite great pressure by the West, which has told him to forget about economic aid without democratic reform.
In the capital Belgrade, where Zajedno's election victory was nullified, non-stop student protests stretched into a fifth day on Thursday in cat-and-mouse games with riot police.

Protesters' sudden appearances and disappearances in different parts of town kept police racing from district to district to prevent local columns from joining forces for a march into the city centre.

Belgrade's election commissioners, whose earlier ruling that Zajedno indeed won control of local government in the capital is being challenged in court, awarded four more seats to Zajedno on Wednesday, padding its claimed majority.
But the Socialists and their neo-communist allies, the Yugoslav United Left led by Milosevic's powerful wife Mira Markovic, have appealed to the Supreme Court.
"It is a world champion-class legalistic mess, meticulously crafted to exhaust just about everyone -- Zajedno, the students and the West. Sorry, it won't work," a Western diplomat said.
